$-p = \Lambda/\kappa^2$: $\rho = \Lambda/\kappa^2$ and $p = -\rho$, the equation of state $w = -1$. The stress tensor is
the same in every frame, as the energy of empty space must be.
:::

The observed value of $\Lambda$ is tiny in natural units. The second exercise converts it to an energy density and
compares it with the Planck scale.

::: {#exr-gr-lambda-value}
#### The observed cosmological constant

With $\Lambda = 1.1 \times 10^{-52}\,\mathrm{m^{-2}}$, compute $\rho_\Lambda c^2 = \Lambda c^4/(8\pi G_N)$ in $\mathrm{J/m^3}$ and
in $\mathrm{eV^4}$ (using $\hbar c = 1.973 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{eV\,m}$), and compare with the fourth power of the reduced
Planck mass $2.4 \times 10^{27}\,$eV.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\rho_\Lambda c^2 = 5.3 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{J/m^3} = (2.3 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV})^4$, about $7 \times 10^{-121}$ of the Planck
density: the cosmological constant problem, the mismatch between this value and any natural estimate of the vacuum
energy.

```python
Lam, c, G, hbarc, eV = 1.1e-52, 2.99792458e8, 6.674e-11, 1.97327e-7, 1.602177e-19   # hbar c in eV m
rho = Lam*c^4/(8*pi.n()*G)
print("rho_Lambda c^2 = %.2e J/m^3 = %.2e kg/m^3 times c^2" % (rho, rho/c^2))
rho_nat = rho/eV*hbarc^3                                   # eV^4
print("in natural units: %.2e eV^4 = (%.2e eV)^4" % (rho_nat, rho_nat^(1/4)))
MP = 2.435e27                                              # reduced Planck mass (8 pi G)^{-1/2} in eV
print("ratio to M_Pl^4 (reduced Planck mass): %.1e" % (rho_nat/MP^4))
```

*Output:*

```text
rho_Lambda c^2 = 5.30e-10 J/m^3 = 5.89e-27 kg/m^3 times c^2
in natural units: 2.54e-11 eV^4 = (2.25e-03 eV)^4
ratio to M_Pl^4 (reduced Planck mass): 7.2e-121
```
:::

The cosmological constant modifies the Newtonian limit as well. The third exercise finds the extra force it
produces on a test particle near a point mass.

::: {#exr-gr-lambda-newtonian}
#### A repulsive force

Show that with a cosmological constant the trace-reversed equations read $R_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2(T_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12Tg_{\mu\nu}) -
\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ in four dimensions, deduce $\nabla^2\Phi = 4\pi G_N\rho - \Lambda$, and find the potential of a point
mass.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The trace of $G_{\mu\nu} - \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2T_{\mu\nu}$ gives $R = -\kappa^2T - 4\Lambda$, and then $R_{\mu\nu} =
\kappa^2T_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} + \tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu}$ is the stated form. Its $tt$ component in the weak field is
$\nabla^2\Phi = 4\pi G_N\rho - \Lambda$, solved outside a point mass by $\Phi = -G_NM/r - \Lambda r^2/6$: an attraction
plus a repulsion $\Lambda r/3$ growing with distance. Indeed $g_{tt} = 1 + 2\Phi = 1 - 2G_NM/r - \Lambda r^2/3$ is the
exact solution of @exr-gr-schwarzschild-de-sitter.
:::
::::

Without matter the Einstein equations still have many solutions, and those of highest symmetry serve as vacua. The
definition records the vacuum equations in their trace-reversed form, which says that the metric is an Einstein
metric.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vacuum-solution}
#### Vacuum solution

A **vacuum solution** of the Einstein equations has $T_{\mu\nu} = 0$: $G_{\mu\nu} - \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = 0$, equivalently
$R_{\mu\nu} = -\tfrac{2\Lambda}{n - 2}g_{\mu\nu}$ in $n$ dimensions (the sign is that of our signature, in which
$g_{tt} > 0$), so that a vacuum solution is an Einstein metric
(@def-einstein-metric). The maximally symmetric vacuum solutions are Minkowski space ($\Lambda = 0$), de Sitter
space ($\Lambda > 0$) and anti-de Sitter space ($\Lambda < 0$) [@carroll1997, p. 228].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
De Sitter space is the vacuum with positive cosmological constant. Its curvature is computed in three and in four
dimensions.

::: {#exm-vacuum-de-sitter}
#### De Sitter space

In three dimensions, with the Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^t_{xx} = \Gamma^t_{yy} = He^{2Ht}$, $\Gamma^x_{tx} =
\Gamma^y_{ty} = H$ (all others zero) one computes, as in @sec-ricci, $R_{\mu\nu} = -2H^2g_{\mu\nu}$ and $R = -6H^2$, hence
$G_{\mu\nu} - H^2g_{\mu\nu} = 0$: de Sitter space is the vacuum solution with $\Lambda = H^2$ (@prp-de-sitter). In
four dimensions, $R_{\mu\nu} = -3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, $R = -12H^2$ and $\Lambda = 3H^2$ (@exr-de-sitter-4d): the Hubble rate of
the expansion is set by the cosmological constant.
:::

The three- and four-dimensional cases are instances of a single formula. The next example gives it in any dimension
$n$ for a metric of constant curvature.

::: {#exm-vacuum-einstein-n}
#### Einstein metrics in $n$ dimensions

For $R_{\mu\nu} = -(n - 1)H^2g_{\mu\nu}$ one has $R = -n(n - 1)H^2$ and $G_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12(n - 1)(n - 2)H^2g_{\mu\nu}$:
for $n = 3$, $G_{\mu\nu} = H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, and for $n = 4$, $G_{\mu\nu} = 3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, in agreement with the two
computations of @exm-vacuum-de-sitter.
:::

The same equations with the opposite sign of the curvature describe internal spheres. This is the mechanism behind
the compactifications of the last part.

::: {#exm-vacuum-sphere-internal}
#### A sphere as internal space

In Part VI the internal sphere of a compactification is an Einstein space with $R_{mn} = (n - 1)R_0^{-2}\gamma_{mn}$
for the positive-definite round metric $\gamma_{mn}$ (@exm-einstein-spheres), that is $R_{mn} = -(n - 1)R_0^{-2}g_{mn}$
for the internal metric $g_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}$ of our signature, and the Einstein equations relate its radius $R_0$
to the flux or cosmological constant
that supports it (the Freund-Rubin mechanism): the same computation as for de Sitter space with the sign of the
curvature reversed.
:::

Anti-de Sitter space, met in @exr-gr-anti-de-sitter in the Poincaré coordinates, is also a hyperboloid, in a flat space
with two times. The next example gives its global coordinates, which show its unusual causal structure.

::: {#exm-grb-ads-global}
#### Global anti-de Sitter space

Four-dimensional anti-de Sitter space of unit radius is the quadric $U^2 + V^2 - X^2 - Y^2 - Z^2 = 1$ in the flat space with metric
$dU^2 + dV^2 - dX^2 - dY^2 - dZ^2$. With $U = \cosh\lambda\cos\alpha$, $V = \cosh\lambda\sin\alpha$ and $(X, Y, Z) = \sinh\lambda\,\hat{\mathbf n}$,
$$
ds^2 = \cosh^2\lambda\,d\alpha^2 - d\lambda^2 - \sinh^2\lambda\,d\Omega^2 .
$$
The time $\alpha$ is periodic, so the quadric has closed timelike curves, and one passes to its universal cover, $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. A
radial light ray has $d\lambda = \cosh\lambda\,d\alpha$, so $\alpha = 2\arctan(\tanh(\lambda/2))$: it reaches $\lambda = \infty$ after the finite
time $\alpha = \pi/2$. The boundary at infinity is at a finite distance for light, the property on which the AdS/CFT
correspondence is built [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.86].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The vacuum equations fix the scalar curvature in terms of $\Lambda$. The first exercise works this out in four
dimensions.

::: {#exr-gr-vacuum-trace}
#### The curvature of a vacuum

Show that a four-dimensional vacuum solution has $R = -4\Lambda$ and $R_{\mu\nu} = -\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$, and check these for
de Sitter space with $\Lambda = 3H^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The trace of $R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu} = \Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ is $-R = 4\Lambda$; substituting back, $R_{\mu\nu} = \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} +
\tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu} = -\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$, the case $n = 4$ of @def-vacuum-solution. For de Sitter space $R = -12H^2 =
-4\Lambda$ and $R_{\mu\nu} = -3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, in agreement (@exr-de-sitter-4d).
:::

Anti-de Sitter space is the vacuum with negative cosmological constant. The second exercise computes its curvature
in Poincaré coordinates with SageManifolds.

::: {#exr-gr-anti-de-sitter}
#### Anti-de Sitter space

Show that $ds^2 = \tfrac{\ell^2}{z^2}(dt^2 - dx^2 - dy^2 - dz^2)$ on $z > 0$ has $R_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac{3}{\ell^2}g_{\mu\nu}$ and solves
the vacuum equations with $\Lambda = -3/\ell^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The metric is conformally flat, and SageManifolds gives $R_{\mu\nu} = 3\ell^{-2}g_{\mu\nu}$, $R = 12/\ell^2$. By
@exr-gr-vacuum-trace, $R_{\mu\nu} = -\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ with $\Lambda = -3/\ell^2 < 0$: the curvature has the opposite sign to
de Sitter space, as for the hyperbolic plane compared with the sphere.

```python
import os, sys; sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))); from _curvature import *
l = var('l'); assume(l > 0)
M, X, g = chart_metric('t x y z', lambda c: [[l^2/c[3]^2, 0, 0, 0], [0, -l^2/c[3]^2, 0, 0], [0, 0, -l^2/c[3]^2, 0], [0, 0, 0, -l^2/c[3]^2]], structure='Lorentzian', ranges='t x y z:(0,+oo)')
Ric, Rs = g.ricci(), g.ricci_scalar()
print("Ricci = (3/l^2) g:", Ric - (3/l^2)*g == 0, "; R =", Rs.expr().simplify_full())
print("G - Lambda g = 0 with Lambda = -3/l^2:", Ric - (Rs/2)*g + (3/l^2)*g == 0)
```

*Output:*

```text
Ricci = (3/l^2) g: True ; R = 12/l^2
G - Lambda g = 0 with Lambda = -3/l^2: True
```
:::

Vacuum solutions need not be maximally symmetric. The third exercise checks a black hole in a universe with a
cosmological constant, combining this section with @sec-schwarzschild-flrw.

::: {#exr-gr-schwarzschild-de-sitter}
#### Schwarzschild-de Sitter

Show that $ds^2 = f\,dt^2 - f^{-1}dr^2 - r^2d\Omega^2$ with $f = 1 - 2m/r - \Lambda r^2/3$ satisfies $R_{\mu\nu} = -\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
SageManifolds gives $R_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = 0$ and $R = -4\Lambda$. For $\Lambda = 0$ this is the Schwarzschild metric of
@def-gr-schwarzschild-metric, for $m = 0$ the static patch of de Sitter space (@exr-gr-int-de-sitter-three-ways); the
weak-field reading of $f$ is the potential of @exr-gr-lambda-newtonian.

```python
import os, sys; sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))); from _curvature import *
m, Lam = var('m Lam')
M, X, g = chart_metric('t r th ph', lambda c: [[1 - 2*m/c[1] - Lam*c[1]^2/3, 0, 0, 0], [0, -1/(1 - 2*m/c[1] - Lam*c[1]^2/3), 0, 0], [0, 0, -c[1]^2, 0], [0, 0, 0, -c[1]^2*sin(c[2])^2]], structure='Lorentzian', ranges='t r:(0,+oo) th:(0,pi) ph:(0,2*pi)')
Ric = g.ricci()
print("R_mu nu + Lambda g_mu nu = 0:", Ric + Lam*g == 0, "; R =", g.ricci_scalar().expr().simplify_full())
```

*Output:*

```text
R_mu nu + Lambda g_mu nu = 0: True ; R = -4*Lam
```
:::

The embedding of the previous example makes the light rays of anti-de Sitter space simple. The next exercise shows
that they are straight lines of the flat ambient space, by a Lagrange multiplier argument.

::: {#exr-grb-ads-null}
#### Light rays are straight lines

Show that the geodesics of the quadric $X\cdot X = 1$ of @exm-grb-ads-global, with $X\cdot Y = \eta_{ab}X^aY^b$ the ambient metric, are the
extremals of $\int\bigl(\tfrac12\dot X\cdot\dot X + \lambda(X\cdot X - 1)\bigr)d\sigma$, that $\dot X\cdot\dot X$ is constant along them, and that the null ones obey
$\ddot X^a = 0$: they are straight lines $X = A + \sigma B$ with $A\cdot A = 1$, $A\cdot B = 0$, $B\cdot B = 0$
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.86].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The multiplier enforces the constraint, and the extremals of the constrained energy functional are the geodesics of the
induced metric. The Euler-Lagrange equation is $\ddot X^a = 2\lambda X^a$. Differentiating $X\cdot X = 1$ twice gives $X\cdot\dot X = 0$ and $\dot X\cdot\dot X +
X\cdot\ddot X = 0$, so $2\lambda = -\dot X\cdot\dot X$; and $\tfrac{d}{d\sigma}(\dot X\cdot\dot X) = 2\dot X\cdot\ddot X = 4\lambda X\cdot\dot X = 0$. For a null geodesic $\dot X\cdot\dot X = 0$,
hence $\lambda = 0$ and $\ddot X = 0$. The line $A + \sigma B$ stays on the quadric for all $\sigma$ iff $A\cdot A = 1$, $A\cdot B = 0$ and $B\cdot B = 0$. Timelike
geodesics, with $\dot X\cdot\dot X = 1$, obey $\ddot X = -X$ instead: they are ellipses $A\cos\sigma + B\sin\sigma$, all returning to their starting
point after $\sigma = 2\pi$, which is why anti-de Sitter space acts like a box for massive particles.
:::
::::

In two dimensions the Einstein tensor vanishes because the Ricci tensor and half the scalar curvature times the metric
cancel exactly. The proposition states this on the unit sphere, and @exr-einstein-2d proves it for every metric.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-einstein-2d}
#### The Einstein tensor vanishes in two dimensions

On the unit sphere $R_{ij} - \tfrac12R\,g_{ij} = 0$ on the chart domain. The same holds for an arbitrary
two-dimensional metric (@exr-einstein-2d).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A flat two-dimensional metric satisfies the proposition trivially, since every curvature tensor vanishes. The flat torus
is the compact example in two dimensions.

::: {#exm-gr-2d-torus}
#### The flat torus

On the flat torus of @exm-riemann-torus all curvature vanishes, $R_{ij} = 0$ and $R = 0$, so $G_{ij} = 0$ without any
cancellation; the Gauss-Bonnet integral is $4\pi\chi = 0$ (@exr-eh-topological).
:::

The interesting cases are curved metrics, where $R_{ij}$ and $\tfrac12Rg_{ij}$ are both non-zero and cancel. The radius
of a sphere shows that the vacuum equations cannot even fix the size of a two-dimensional space.

::: {#exm-gr-2d-sphere-radius}
#### A sphere of any radius

For the round sphere of radius $a$, $R_{ij} = a^{-2}g_{ij}$ and $R = 2/a^2$ (@exm-sphere-curvature-radius), so $G_{ij} =
a^{-2}g_{ij} - a^{-2}g_{ij} = 0$ for every $a$: no equation selects the radius.
:::

Two-dimensional de Sitter space, drawn in @fig-de-sitter, is a Lorentzian example. It is curved but has zero
Einstein tensor, as computed in @exr-gr-2d-ds2.

::: {#exm-gr-2d-ds2}
#### Two-dimensional de Sitter space

$ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2Ht}dx^2$ has $R_{\mu\nu} = -H^2g_{\mu\nu}$ and $R = -2H^2$, the case $n = 2$ of
@exm-vacuum-einstein-n, whose formula $G_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12(n - 1)(n - 2)H^2g_{\mu\nu}$ indeed vanishes at $n = 2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the Lorentzian example with SageManifolds. It confirms the values of the Ricci tensor and
the scalar curvature quoted in the last example.

::: {#exr-gr-2d-ds2}
#### De Sitter space in two dimensions

Compute the Ricci tensor, the scalar curvature and the Einstein tensor of $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2Ht}dx^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The only non-zero Christoffel symbols are $\Gamma^t_{xx} = He^{2Ht}$ and $\Gamma^x_{tx} = H$; the Ricci tensor is $-H^2g$, the
scalar curvature $-2H^2$ and the Einstein tensor zero.

```python
import os, sys; sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))); from _curvature import *
H = var('H'); assume(H > 0)
M, X, g = chart_metric('t x', lambda c: [[1, 0], [0, -exp(2*H*c[0])]], structure='Lorentzian')
Ric, Rs = g.ricci(), g.ricci_scalar()
print("Ricci = -H^2 g:", Ric + H^2*g == 0, "; R =", Rs.expr().simplify_full(), "; G = Ric - R g/2 = 0:", Ric - (Rs/2)*g == 0)
```

*Output:*

```text
Ricci = -H^2 g: True ; R = -2*H^2 ; G = Ric - R g/2 = 0: True
```
:::

The second exercise, from the old version of this section, proves the statement for every two-dimensional metric.
Its solution uses the single independent component of the Riemann tensor and computes a generic metric explicitly.

::: {#exr-einstein-2d}
#### Two dimensions

Show that the Einstein tensor of an arbitrary two-dimensional metric vanishes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In two dimensions the Riemann tensor has one independent component and $R_{ijkl} = \tfrac12R(g_{ik}g_{jl} -
g_{il}g_{jk})$ (@sec-riemann); contracting, $R_{jl} = \tfrac12R\,g_{jl}$, so $G_{jl} = 0$. In Sage, for a generic
symmetric metric with three arbitrary functions, built as a SageManifolds metric:

```python
import os, sys; sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))); from _curvature import *
M = Manifold(2, 'M', structure='Riemannian'); X = M.chart('u v'); u, v = X[:]
A = function('A')(u, v); B = function('B')(u, v); C = function('C')(u, v)      # a generic symmetric 2x2 metric
g = M.metric('g'); g[0, 0] = A; g[0, 1] = B; g[1, 1] = C
Ric, Rs = g.ricci(), g.ricci_scalar()
G = Ric - (Rs/2)*g
print("Einstein tensor of a generic 2D metric:", G.display())
print("[G_ij = 0 identically]:", G == 0)
```

*Output:*

```text
Einstein tensor of a generic 2D metric: Ric(g)-unnamed metric = 0
[G_ij = 0 identically]: True
```

:::

Three dimensions are the next special case: there the Einstein equations have content, but no gravitational waves.
The third exercise explains why by counting components.

::: {#exr-gr-3d-flat}
#### Three-dimensional gravity

Show that in three dimensions the Riemann tensor has as many independent components as the Ricci tensor, and deduce
that every solution of the vacuum equations with $\Lambda = 0$ is flat.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Riemann tensor has $n^2(n^2 - 1)/12 = 6$ components for $n = 3$, and the symmetric Ricci tensor has $n(n + 1)/2 =
6$. In fact $R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ is a linear combination of $R_{\mu\rho}g_{\nu\sigma}$-type terms and $Rg_{\mu\rho}g_{\nu\sigma}$-type
terms. In vacuum with $\Lambda = 0$, $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$ (@exr-gr-trace-reversed), hence $R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = 0$: the metric is flat
locally, and gravity in three dimensions has no local degrees of freedom. Massive objects only produce a conical
deficit angle.
:::
::::

De Sitter space in three dimensions is small enough to be computed completely, from the metric to the field
equation. The proposition records the inverse metric, the connection, the curvature and the vacuum equation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-de-sitter}
#### Curvature of three-dimensional de Sitter space

For $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2Ht}(dx^2 + dy^2)$: the inverse metric is $\operatorname{diag}(1, -e^{-2Ht}, -e^{-2Ht})$, the
Christoffel symbols are as stated in @exm-vacuum-de-sitter, $R_{\mu\nu} = -2H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, $R = -6H^2$ and $G_{\mu\nu} -
H^2g_{\mu\nu} = 0$, everywhere, since $e^{2Ht} \neq 0$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The coordinate $t$ of de Sitter space is the proper time of the comoving observers. Their separation grows
exponentially at a constant rate.

::: {#exm-gr-ds-hubble}
#### A constant Hubble rate

Two comoving observers at fixed $x$ and $x + \Delta x$ are at physical distance $d = e^{Ht}\Delta x$ at time $t$, so $\dot d
= Hd$: they recede at a speed proportional to their distance, with the constant Hubble rate $H = \dot a/a$ and
$a = e^{Ht}$ (@def-gr-flrw-metric).
:::

Exponential expansion hides part of the universe from every observer. The light rays of the flat slicing make this
explicit.

::: {#exm-gr-ds-horizon}
#### The cosmological horizon

A light ray $dx/dt = e^{-Ht}$ sent at time $t$ from $x = 0$ reaches at most the comoving coordinate $\int_t^\infty
e^{-Ht'}dt' = e^{-Ht}/H$, the physical distance $1/H$. Events farther away than $1/H$ can never be influenced by the
observer: de Sitter space has a horizon, which in static coordinates is the surface $r = 1/H$ of
@exr-gr-int-de-sitter-three-ways.
:::

The flat slicing covers only half of de Sitter space. The full space is the hyperboloid of @fig-de-sitter, on which
the symmetry is manifest.

![Two-dimensional de Sitter space as the hyperboloid $X_0^2 - X_1^2 - X_2^2 = -1/H^2$ in three-dimensional
Minkowski space, with the flat-slicing coordinates: surfaces of constant $t$ (red circles, growing like $e^{Ht}$)
and lines of constant $x$ (blue). The induced metric is $dt^2 - e^{2Ht}dx^2$.](figures/de_sitter.png){#fig-de-sitter width=55%}

::: {#exm-gr-ds-hyperboloid}
#### The hyperboloid

$n$-dimensional de Sitter space is the hyperboloid $X_0^2 - X_1^2 - \dots - X_n^2 = -1/H^2$ in $(n + 1)$-dimensional
Minkowski space, and the Lorentz group $SO(1, n)$ of the ambient space acts on it by isometries: dimension $n(n + 1)/2$,
the maximum (@def-maximally-symmetric). The flat slicing covers the half $X_0 + X_n > 0$, as @fig-de-sitter shows for
$n = 2$.
:::

In the flat slicing the geodesics of de Sitter space are simple too. The next example shows that free particles and
light move on straight lines of the comoving coordinates, the expansion acting only on the speed.

::: {#exm-grb-ds-straight}
#### Straight comoving paths

For $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2t/R}(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2)$ the metric does not depend on $\mathbf x$, so $e^{2t/R}\,d\mathbf x/d\tau = \mathbf p$ is constant along
a geodesic. The direction of $d\mathbf x/d\tau$ is fixed: free particles and photons move on straight lines in the comoving
coordinates. A photon sent from $x = X$ towards the origin at $t = 0$ has $dx/dt = -e^{-t/R}$ and arrives at $t = -R\log(1 - X/R)$ if
$X < R$, never if $X \geq R$, the horizon of @exm-gr-ds-horizon [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.83].
:::

Global coordinates on the hyperboloid show the same horizon from another angle. The next example follows light on the
two-dimensional de Sitter space, where the whole spacetime can be drawn.

::: {#exm-grb-ds2-global}
#### Light on the two-dimensional hyperboloid

On $x_0^2 - x_1^2 - x_2^2 = -1$ in three-dimensional Minkowski space, $x_0 = \sinh\tau$, $x_1 = \cosh\tau\cos\varphi$, $x_2 = \cosh\tau\sin\varphi$ give
$ds^2 = d\tau^2 - \cosh^2\tau\,d\varphi^2$. A light ray has $d\varphi = d\tau/\cosh\tau$, so $\varphi(\tau) - \varphi(\tau_0) = \operatorname{gd}\tau - \operatorname{gd}\tau_0$ with the
Gudermannian $\operatorname{gd}\tau = 2\arctan(\tanh(\tau/2))$, which runs from $-\pi/2$ to $\pi/2$. Over the whole history of the universe a
ray covers half the circle; sent at $x_0 = 0$ from $\varphi = 0$ it reaches $\varphi = \pi/2$ only as $x_0 \to \infty$, and the antipodal half
of the circle never receives it [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.79].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise, from the old version of this section, extends the computation of @prp-de-sitter to four dimensions.
It gives the value $\Lambda = 3H^2$ used in cosmology.

::: {#exr-de-sitter-4d}
#### Four-dimensional de Sitter space

Compute the Ricci tensor and scalar curvature of $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2Ht}d\mathbf x^2$ in four dimensions and find
$\Lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The non-zero symbols are $\Gamma^t_{ij} = He^{2Ht}\delta_{ij}$ and $\Gamma^i_{tj} = H\delta^i_j$; the Ricci tensor is
$-3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, $R = -12H^2$, $G_{\mu\nu} = 3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$ and $\Lambda = 3H^2$. In Sage:

```python
import os, sys; sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))); from _curvature import *
H = var('H', domain='real'); assume(H > 0)
M, X, g = chart_metric('t x y z', lambda c: [[1, 0, 0, 0], [0, -exp(2*H*c[0]), 0, 0], [0, 0, -exp(2*H*c[0]), 0], [0, 0, 0, -exp(2*H*c[0])]], structure='Lorentzian')
Ric, Rs = g.ricci(), g.ricci_scalar()
print("Ricci tensor = -3 H^2 g:", (Ric + 3*H**2*g) == 0, "; scalar curvature R =", Rs.expr().simplify_full())
G = Ric - (Rs/2)*g
print("Einstein tensor G - 3 H^2 g = 0 (Lambda = 3 H^2):", (G - 3*H**2*g) == 0)
```

*Output:*

```text
Ricci tensor = -3 H^2 g: True ; scalar curvature R = -12*H^2
Einstein tensor G - 3 H^2 g = 0 (Lambda = 3 H^2): True
```
:::

Geodesics of de Sitter space other than the comoving ones slow down. The second exercise shows that the momentum of
a free particle decays like $1/a$.

::: {#exr-gr-ds-peculiar}
#### Peculiar velocities decay

For a geodesic of $ds^2 = dt^2 - a(t)^2d\mathbf x^2$, show that $a^2\,dx^i/d\tau$ is constant, using that $g$ does not depend on
$x^i$. Deduce that the momentum measured by comoving observers, $p = ma\,|d\mathbf x/d\tau|$, decreases as $1/a$; what does this
mean for de Sitter space?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_i$ is a Killing vector, so $g(\partial_i, u) = -a^2\,dx^i/d\tau$ is conserved along geodesics (as for $E$ in
@exr-gr-nl-energy). Hence $a\,|d\mathbf x/d\tau| \propto 1/a$ and $p \propto 1/a$. In de Sitter space $a = e^{Ht}$, so any
initial motion relative to the comoving observers dies away exponentially, and the comoving geodesics of
@exm-equivalence-geodesics are attractors. For light the same law is the cosmological redshift (@exr-gr-flrw-redshift).
:::

Translations in time are not obviously symmetries of the flat slicing, because the metric depends on $t$. The third
exercise finds the Killing vector that combines a time translation with a dilation.

::: {#exr-gr-ds-killing}
#### A hidden time translation

Show that $\xi = \partial_t - H(x\partial_x + y\partial_y + z\partial_z)$ is a Killing vector of four-dimensional de Sitter space in
flat slicing (@def-killing), while $\partial_t$ is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The finite transformation $t \mapsto t + c$, $\mathbf x \mapsto e^{-Hc}\mathbf x$ maps $e^{2Ht}d\mathbf x^2$ to $e^{2H(t + c)}e^{-2Hc}d\mathbf x^2$,
an isometry; $\xi$ is its generator. SageManifolds gives $\mathcal{L}_\xi g = 0$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\partial_t}g = -2He^{2Ht}d\mathbf x^2 \neq
0$.

```python
import os, sys; sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))); from _curvature import *
H = var('H'); assume(H > 0)
M, X, g = chart_metric('t x y z', lambda c: [[1, 0, 0, 0], [0, -exp(2*H*c[0]), 0, 0], [0, 0, -exp(2*H*c[0]), 0], [0, 0, 0, -exp(2*H*c[0])]], structure='Lorentzian')
t, x, y, z = X[:]
xi = M.vector_field(1, -H*x, -H*y, -H*z, name='xi')
dt = M.vector_field(1, 0, 0, 0, name='dt')
print("L_xi g = 0:", g.lie_derivative(xi) == 0)
print("L_{d_t} g =", g.lie_derivative(dt).display())
```

*Output:*

```text
L_xi g = 0: True
L_{d_t} g = -2*H*e^(2*H*t) dx⊗dx - 2*H*e^(2*H*t) dy⊗dy - 2*H*e^(2*H*t) dz⊗dz
```
:::

Redshifts between comoving observers measure the expansion. The next exercise computes the redshift in two-dimensional
de Sitter space exactly, including the horizon beyond which no signal arrives.

::: {#exr-grb-ds2-redshift}
#### Redshift in de Sitter space

In $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2t/R}dx^2$ a comoving observer at $x_0$ emits light at time $t_e$ towards a comoving observer at $x_1 = x_0 + d$. With
Sage, find the arrival time and show that $1 + z = \bigl(1 - de^{t_e/R}/R\bigr)^{-1}$. What happens when $de^{t_e/R} \geq R$, and what is
$z$ for small $d$? [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.139]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Along the ray $dx/dt = e^{-t/R}$, and the frequency scales as $1/a$ (@exr-gr-flrw-redshift):

```python
t, te, tr, R, x0, x1, d = var('t te tr R x0 x1 d'); assume(R > 0, d > 0)
a = exp(t / R)
# null ray dx/dt = 1/a: x1 - x0 = int_te^tr exp(-t/R) dt
travel = integrate(exp(-t / R), t, te, tr)
sol = solve(travel == d, tr)[0].rhs()
print("arrival time tr =", sol)
z1 = (a.subs(t=sol) / a.subs(t=te)).simplify_full()
print("1 + z =", z1)
print("1 + z equals 1/(1 - d exp(te/R)/R):", bool((z1 - 1 / (1 - d * exp(te / R) / R)).simplify_full() == 0))
print("small separation: z = d exp(te/R)/R + O(d^2):", bool(taylor(z1 - 1, d, 0, 1) == d * exp(te / R) / R))
```

*Output:*

```text
arrival time tr = R*log(-R*e^(te/R)/(d*e^(te/R) - R))
1 + z = -R/(d*e^(te/R) - R)
1 + z equals 1/(1 - d exp(te/R)/R): True
small separation: z = d exp(te/R)/R + O(d^2): True
```

For $de^{t_e/R} \geq R$ the light never arrives: the receiver is beyond the horizon of the emission event. For small $d$, $z =
He^{t_e/R}d$ with $H = 1/R$, Hubble's law with the proper distance $e^{t_e/R}d$.
:::

A field on de Sitter space feels the expansion as friction. The next exercise computes the wave operator and finds its
simplest solutions, which show the damping explicitly.

::: {#exr-grb-ds2-wave}
#### Waves on two-dimensional de Sitter space

With Sage, compute $\Box\Phi = g^{\mu\nu}\nabla_\mu\nabla_\nu\Phi$ for $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2t/R}dx^2$. Find the solutions that do not depend on $x$, and
show that $e^{ik(x - \eta)}$ with the conformal time $\eta = -Re^{-t/R}$ is a solution. [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.140]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
SageManifolds gives the operator, and the two families of solutions are checked by substitution:

```python
M = Manifold(2, 'M', structure='Lorentzian'); X.<t, x> = M.chart(); R = var('R'); assume(R > 0)
g = M.metric('g'); g[0, 0] = 1; g[1, 1] = -exp(2 * t / R)
Phi = M.scalar_field(function('Phi')(t, x), name='Phi')
nab = g.connection(); H = nab(Phi.differential()); gi = g.inverse()
box = sum(gi[a, b].expr() * H[a, b].expr() for a in range(2) for b in range(2))   # g^{ab} nabla_a nabla_b Phi
print("Box Phi =", box.simplify_full())
expected = diff(function('Phi')(t, x), t, 2) + diff(function('Phi')(t, x), t) / R - exp(-2 * t / R) * diff(function('Phi')(t, x), x, 2)
print("Box Phi = Phi_tt + Phi_t/R - exp(-2t/R) Phi_xx:", bool((box - expected).simplify_full() == 0))
A, B, k, eta = var('A B k eta')
f = A + B * exp(-t / R)
print("homogeneous solutions A + B exp(-t/R):", bool((diff(f, t, 2) + diff(f, t) / R).simplify_full() == 0))
w = exp(I * k * x) * exp(-I * k * (-R * exp(-t / R)))   # exp(i k (x - eta)) with eta = -R exp(-t/R)
print("exp(i k (x - eta)) solves the wave equation:", bool((diff(w, t, 2) + diff(w, t) / R - exp(-2 * t / R) * diff(w, x, 2)).simplify_full() == 0))
```

*Output:*

```text
Box Phi = (R*e^(2*t/R)*diff(Phi(t, x), t, t) + e^(2*t/R)*diff(Phi(t, x), t) - R*diff(Phi(t, x), x, x))*e^(-2*t/R)/R
Box Phi = Phi_tt + Phi_t/R - exp(-2t/R) Phi_xx: True
homogeneous solutions A + B exp(-t/R): True
exp(i k (x - eta)) solves the wave equation: True
```

The term $\Phi_t/R = H\Phi_t$ is Hubble friction: homogeneous solutions settle to a constant, $A + Be^{-t/R}$. In conformal time
$ds^2 = e^{2t/R}(d\eta^2 - dx^2)$ is conformally flat, and in two dimensions $\sqrt{|g|}g^{\mu\nu}$ is conformally invariant, so the
massless wave equation is the flat one, $\partial_\eta^2\Phi - \partial_x^2\Phi = 0$.
:::
::::

## Black holes and cosmology {#sec-schwarzschild-flrw}

The Einstein equations are non-linear, and exact solutions exist only under strong symmetry assumptions. Two of them
carry most of the observable content of the theory. Outside a spherically symmetric mass the solution is unique, the
Schwarzschild metric; it contains a horizon, describes black holes, and its geodesics give the perihelion advance of
Mercury and the bending of light. Its symmetries, the Killing vectors of the mathematics part, give the conserved
quantities that make the orbits solvable and the redshift and time delay of light exact, the last two of the four
classical tests. A charged mass is described by the Reissner-Nordström solution of the coupled Einstein and Maxwell
equations, the four-dimensional theory that Kaluza-Klein reduction produces. A homogeneous and isotropic universe is
described by the FLRW metric, whose single function $a(t)$ obeys the Friedmann equations. In this section we keep $G_N$ explicit in the definitions and set $G_N = c
= 1$ in computations, writing $m = G_NM$ for the mass in units of length.

For more on this topic, see @boskoff2024journey [Ch. 10], @buchbinder2021introduction [Sec. 11.7] and @godinho2014introduction [Ch. 6].

### The Schwarzschild solution

The simplest source of gravity is a single spherical body, and the simplest region to study is the empty space
around it. There the vacuum equations $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$ must hold, and spherical symmetry reduces them to ordinary
differential equations whose solution was found by Schwarzschild in 1916.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gr-schwarzschild-metric}
#### Schwarzschild metric

The **Schwarzschild metric** of mass $M > 0$ is
$$
ds^2 = \Bigl(1 - \frac{2G_NM}{r}\Bigr)dt^2 - \Bigl(1 - \frac{2G_NM}{r}\Bigr)^{-1}dr^2 - r^2\bigl(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2\bigr),
$$ {#eq-gr-schwarzschild}
on $r > 2G_NM$, where $r$ is defined by the area $4\pi r^2$ of the spheres of constant $t$ and $r$. It is a vacuum solution,
$R_{\mu\nu} = 0$ (@prp-gr-schwarzschild), and by **Birkhoff's theorem** it is the only spherically symmetric one: the
gravitational field outside any spherical body is @eq-gr-schwarzschild
[@carroll1997, ch. 7, with the overall sign of our signature]. The radius $r_s = 2G_NM$ is the **Schwarzschild radius**.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Far from the mass the metric must reduce to the weak field of @def-newtonian-limit. The time component does so
directly.

::: {#exm-gr-schw-newtonian}
#### The Newtonian potential

At large $r$, $g_{tt} = 1 - 2G_NM/r = 1 + 2\Phi$ with $\Phi = -G_NM/r$, the Newtonian potential of a point mass
(@exm-newtonian-point-mass). The radial component $g_{rr} = -(1 + 2G_NM/r + \dots)$ differs from the $-(1 - 2\Phi)$ of
@prp-newtonian-limit only by the choice of radial coordinate, as @exr-gr-schw-isotropic shows.
:::

The Schwarzschild radius is small for ordinary bodies. Comparing it with their actual radii shows why the horizon plays
no role in the solar system.

::: {#exm-gr-schw-radius}
#### Schwarzschild radii

With $G_NM_\odot/c^2 = 1.48\,$km, the Sun has $r_s = 2.95\,$km, far inside its radius of $696\,000\,$km where the vacuum
solution does not apply; the Earth has $r_s = 8.9\,$mm. Only bodies compressed below $r_s$, black holes, have the
surface $r = 2G_NM$ outside them.
:::

Birkhoff's theorem has a striking consequence for dynamics. Whatever a spherical star does internally, its exterior
gravitational field cannot change at all.

::: {#exm-gr-schw-birkhoff}
#### No spherical waves

A spherically symmetric star that pulsates or collapses keeps the exterior metric @eq-gr-schwarzschild with constant $M$:
there is no spherically symmetric gravitational radiation, just as there is no monopole electromagnetic radiation.
Gravitational waves need a changing quadrupole moment.
:::

The Schwarzschild metric is curved, yet it can be drawn as a surface in a flat space of higher dimension. The next
example gives Fronsdal's embedding into six-dimensional Minkowski space.

::: {#exm-grb-fronsdal}
#### An embedding in six dimensions

With $r_s = 2G_NM$, set $Z_1 = 2r_s\sinh\frac{t}{2r_s}f(r)$, $Z_2 = 2r_s\cosh\frac{t}{2r_s}f(r)$, $Z_3 = g(r)$ and $(Z_4, Z_5, Z_6) = r\,\hat{\mathbf n}(\theta, \varphi)$
in the space with metric $dZ_1^2 - dZ_2^2 - \dots - dZ_6^2$. Then $dZ_1^2 - dZ_2^2 = f^2dt^2 - 4r_s^2f'^2dr^2$, and @eq-gr-schwarzschild is reproduced
by $f = \sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$ and
$$
g'(r)^2 = \frac{r_s}{r}\Bigl(1 + \frac{r_s}{r} + \frac{r_s^2}{r^2}\Bigr),
$$
since then $4r_s^2f'^2 + g'^2 + 1 = (1 - r_s/r)^{-1}$. The embedding is regular at $r = r_s$, where $f = 0$: the horizon is the
intersection with $Z_1 = \pm Z_2$, a first sign that it is not a singularity [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.77].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The size of a black hole of given mass follows from the definition. The first exercise computes a few, from stellar
to galactic masses.

::: {#exr-gr-schw-radius-numbers}
#### Black holes of different masses

Compute $r_s = 2G_NM/c^2$ for a black hole of $10$ solar masses and for Sagittarius A$^*$, the black hole at the centre of
the Galaxy, of $4.3 \times 10^6$ solar masses, and compare the latter with the radius of the Earth's orbit, $1.5 \times
10^8\,$km. What is the mean density inside $r_s$, as a function of $M$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$r_s = 2.95\,$km per solar mass: $29.5\,$km and $1.27 \times 10^7\,$km, about $0.085$ of the Earth-Sun distance. The mean
density $M/(\tfrac43\pi r_s^3) = 3c^6/(32\pi G_N^3M^2)$ decreases as $M^{-2}$: a stellar black hole is denser than a nucleus,
while one of $10^8$ solar masses has the density of water.
:::

That $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$ does not mean that space is flat: the Riemann tensor carries the tidal field. The second
exercise computes one component with SageManifolds.

::: {#exr-gr-schw-ricci-flat}
#### Ricci flat but curved

Compute the Ricci tensor of @eq-gr-schwarzschild (with $G_N = 1$, $m = M$) and the component $R^r{}_{trt}$ of the Riemann
tensor, and compare the latter with the radial tidal acceleration of @exr-gr-tidal.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R_{\mu\nu} = 0$ and $R = 0$, but $R^r{}_{trt} = -2m(r - 2m)/r^4 = -\tfrac{2m}{r^3}(1 - 2m/r)$. For a particle momentarily at
rest, $u^t = (1 - 2m/r)^{-1/2}$, and geodesic deviation in the radial direction gives $\ddot\xi^r = R^r{}_{ttr}(u^t)^2\xi^r = -
R^r{}_{trt}(u^t)^2\xi^r = \tfrac{2m}{r^3}\xi^r$: the radial stretching $2G_NM/r^3$ of @exr-gr-tidal.

```python
import os, sys; sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))); from _curvature import *
m = var('m'); assume(m > 0)
M, X, g = chart_metric('t r th ph', lambda c: [[1 - 2*m/c[1], 0, 0, 0], [0, -1/(1 - 2*m/c[1]), 0, 0], [0, 0, -c[1]^2, 0], [0, 0, 0, -c[1]^2*sin(c[2])^2]], structure='Lorentzian', ranges='t r:(0,+oo) th:(0,pi) ph:(0,2*pi)')
Rm, Ric, Rs = curvature(g)
print("R^r_{t r t} =", Rm[1, 0, 1, 0].expr().simplify_full())
print("Ricci tensor vanishes:", Ric == 0, "; scalar curvature:", Rs.expr())
```

*Output:*

```text
R^r_{t r t} = 2*(2*m^2 - m*r)/r^4
Ricci tensor vanishes: True ; scalar curvature: 0
```
:::

Different radial coordinates can make the metric look different. The third exercise finds isotropic coordinates, in
which the spatial part is conformally flat and the weak-field form of @def-newtonian-limit appears exactly.

::: {#exr-gr-schw-isotropic}
#### Isotropic coordinates

Substitute $r = \rho(1 + m/2\rho)^2$ in @eq-gr-schwarzschild and show that the metric becomes $\bigl(\tfrac{1 - m/2\rho}{1 +
m/2\rho}\bigr)^2dt^2 - (1 + m/2\rho)^4(d\rho^2 + \rho^2d\Omega^2)$. Expand to first order in $m$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$1 - 2m/r = \bigl(\tfrac{1 - m/2\rho}{1 + m/2\rho}\bigr)^2$, $dr/d\rho = (1 - m/2\rho)(1 + m/2\rho)$, so $g_{\rho\rho} = -(1 + m/2\rho)^4$, and
$r^2 = \rho^2(1 + m/2\rho)^4$ gives the same factor on the sphere. To first order: $g_{tt} = 1 - 2m/\rho$ and $g_{ij} = -(1 +
2m/\rho)\delta_{ij}$, which is exactly the weak-field metric of @prp-newtonian-limit with $\Phi = -m/\rho$.

```python
m, rho, eps = var('m rho eps'); assume(rho > m/2, m > 0)
r = rho*(1 + m/(2*rho))^2
f = 1 - 2*m/r
gtt = f.simplify_full(); grr = (-(1/f)*diff(r, rho)^2).simplify_full(); gang = (-r^2/rho^2).simplify_full()
print("g_tt =", gtt.factor(), "; equals ((1 - m/2rho)/(1 + m/2rho))^2:", bool((gtt - ((1 - m/(2*rho))/(1 + m/(2*rho)))^2).simplify_full() == 0))
print("g_rho rho = g_angular/rho^2 = -(1 + m/2rho)^4:", bool((grr + (1 + m/(2*rho))^4).simplify_full() == 0), bool((gang + (1 + m/(2*rho))^4).simplify_full() == 0))
lin = lambda e: e.subs(m=eps*m).taylor(eps, 0, 1).subs(eps=1)
print("to first order: g_tt =", lin(gtt).expand(), "; g_rho rho =", lin(grr).expand())
```

*Output:*

```text
g_tt = (m - 2*rho)^2/(m + 2*rho)^2 ; equals ((1 - m/2rho)/(1 + m/2rho))^2: True
g_rho rho = g_angular/rho^2 = -(1 + m/2rho)^4: True True
to first order: g_tt = -2*m/rho + 1 ; g_rho rho = -2*m/rho - 1
```
:::

The Kretschmann scalar of @prp-gr-schwarzschild is finite at $r = 2m$, but a single invariant can hide divergent
components. The next exercise computes all the curvature components that an observer measures, which are the tidal
accelerations.

::: {#exr-grb-frame-curvature}
#### Curvature in the observer's frame

With Sage, compute the components $R_{(abab)}$ of the Riemann tensor of @eq-gr-schwarzschild ($G_N = 1$, $m = M$) in the orthonormal frame
$e_{(t)} = (1 - 2m/r)^{-1/2}\partial_t$, $e_{(r)} = (1 - 2m/r)^{1/2}\partial_r$, $e_{(\theta)} = r^{-1}\partial_\theta$, $e_{(\varphi)} = (r\sin\theta)^{-1}\partial_\varphi$, and check
the Kretschmann scalar. Are they finite at $r = 2m$? What do they mean for a falling body?
[@plebanski2024introduction, Sec. 14.17, Exercise 7; @blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.110]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Dividing the coordinate components by the norms of the coordinate vectors:

```python
M = Manifold(4, 'M', structure='Lorentzian'); X.<t, r, th, ph> = M.chart(r't r:(0,+oo) th:(0,pi):\theta ph:(0,2*pi):\phi')
m = var('m'); assume(m > 0)
g = M.metric('g'); f = 1 - 2 * m / r
g[0, 0] = f; g[1, 1] = -1 / f; g[2, 2] = -r^2; g[3, 3] = -(r * sin(th))^2
Rm = g.riemann().down(g)                       # R_{abcd}
Ru = g.riemann().up(g)                         # R^{abcd}
K = sum(Rm[a, b, c, d] * Ru[a, b, c, d] for a in range(4) for b in range(4) for c in range(4) for d in range(4))
K = K.expr().simplify_full()
print("Kretschmann scalar:", K, "  equals 48 m^2/r^6:", bool(K == 48 * m^2 / r^6))
scale = [sqrt(f), 1 / sqrt(f), r, r * sin(th)]   # |g_aa|^(1/2): orthonormal components R_(abcd) = R_abcd / prod
names = ['t', 'r', 'theta', 'phi']
for (a, b) in [(0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)]:
    comp = (Rm[a, b, a, b].expr() / (scale[a] * scale[b])^2).simplify_full()
    print("R_(%s %s %s %s) =" % (names[a], names[b], names[a], names[b]), comp)
```

*Output:*

```text
Kretschmann scalar: 48*m^2/r^6   equals 48 m^2/r^6: True
R_(t r t r) = 2*m/r^3
R_(t theta t theta) = -m/r^3
R_(t phi t phi) = -m/r^3
R_(r theta r theta) = m/r^3
R_(r phi r phi) = m/r^3
R_(theta phi theta phi) = -2*m/r^3
```

All components are $\pm2m/r^3$ or $\pm m/r^3$, finite at $r = 2m$ and divergent only at $r = 0$; the frame itself is singular at the
horizon, but the components in the frame of a radially falling observer are the same, since radial boosts leave these
components unchanged. By the geodesic deviation equation a body is stretched radially with tidal acceleration $2m/r^3$ per
unit length and compressed sideways with $m/r^3$, as in Newtonian gravity (@exr-gr-tidal); at $r = 0$ the stretching becomes
infinite.
:::
::::

The coefficient $g_{rr}$ blows up at $r = 2G_NM$. This is not a singularity of spacetime but of the coordinates, and the
surface $r = 2G_NM$ has a physical meaning of its own: nothing that crosses it inwards can come back.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gr-event-horizon}
#### Event horizon

The **event horizon** of the Schwarzschild spacetime is the surface $r = 2G_NM$. In the ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein
coordinate $v = t + r_*$, with the tortoise coordinate $r_* = r + 2G_NM\log|r/2G_NM - 1|$, the metric reads
$$
ds^2 = \Bigl(1 - \frac{2G_NM}{r}\Bigr)dv^2 - 2\,dv\,dr - r^2d\Omega^2,
$$ {#eq-gr-eddington-finkelstein}
which is regular at $r = 2G_NM$ and extends the spacetime to $0 < r < 2G_NM$. Inside the horizon every future-directed
timelike or null curve has decreasing $r$; the region $r < 2G_NM$ is a **black hole**, and its boundary is the boundary of
the set of events from which signals can reach infinity [@carroll1997, ch. 7]. The curvature singularity is at
$r = 0$, where $R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = 48G_N^2M^2/r^6$ diverges (@prp-gr-schwarzschild).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The light cones in the Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates show the horizon at work. They are drawn in the left panel
of @fig-schwarzschild.

::: {#exm-gr-horizon-cones}
#### Tilting light cones

In the coordinates $(r, \tilde t = v - r)$ radial light rays have slopes $d\tilde t/dr = -1$ (ingoing) and $(1 + 2m/r)/(1 -
2m/r)$ (outgoing). Outside the horizon the outgoing slope is positive; at $r = 2m$ it is infinite, the ray stays at
$r = 2m$; inside it is negative, so both rays move to smaller $r$. The cones tilt inwards as the horizon is crossed.
:::

In Schwarzschild coordinates the approach to the horizon takes forever. The tortoise coordinate measures how, and
makes the radial light rays straight.

::: {#exm-gr-horizon-tortoise}
#### The tortoise coordinate

Radial light rays obey $dt = \pm dr/(1 - 2m/r) = \pm dr_*$, and $r_* \to -\infty$ as $r \to 2m$: a light ray needs infinite
coordinate time $t$ to reach the horizon. Since $t$ is the time of a distant observer, the infall is never seen to
complete, although it takes finite proper time (@exr-gr-horizon-infall-time).
:::

The horizon is also a surface of infinite redshift. Static clocks near it run arbitrarily slowly compared with
clocks far away.

::: {#exm-gr-horizon-redshift}
#### Infinite redshift

A static source at radius $r$ emitting at frequency $\nu$ is received at infinity at $\nu_\infty = \nu\sqrt{1 - 2m/r}$
(@exm-newtonian-redshift, now exact). As $r \to 2m$ the ratio tends to zero: an object falling in appears to freeze and
fade at the horizon.
:::

Staying at a fixed radius near a black hole requires a rocket. The next example computes the acceleration that the
rocket must provide, which grows without bound at the horizon.

::: {#exm-grb-static-acceleration}
#### Hovering above a black hole

A static observer at radius $r$ has $u = (1 - 2m/r)^{-1/2}\partial_t$, and its four-acceleration $a^\mu = u^\nu\nabla_\nu u^\mu$ has the only component
$a^r = \Gamma^r_{tt}(u^t)^2 = m/r^2$, so the proper acceleration is
$$
\alpha = \sqrt{-g_{rr}}\,a^r = \frac{m}{r^2\sqrt{1 - 2m/r}} .
$$
For $r \gg m$ this is Newton's $G_NM/r^2$; it diverges at $r = 2m$, where no observer can stay at rest. The redshifted value
$\sqrt{1 - 2m/r}\,\alpha \to 1/(4m)$ is the surface gravity of @exr-gr-horizon-temperature [@blennow2022relativity, Problems 2.94 and 2.100].
:::

Inside the horizon every observer reaches $r = 0$ in a finite proper time. The next example computes the longest
possible time, for a fall from rest.

::: {#exm-grb-max-proper-time}
#### The longest fall

Radial free fall from rest at $r_0$ has $E^2 = 1 - 2m/r_0$ and $\dot r^2 = 2m/r - 2m/r_0$, solved by the cycloid $r = \tfrac{r_0}{2}(1 + \cos\eta)$,
$\tau = \sqrt{r_0^3/8m}\,(\eta + \sin\eta)$: the singularity $\eta = \pi$ is reached after $\tau = \pi\sqrt{r_0^3/8m}$, the Newtonian free-fall time. From
the horizon, $r_0 = 2m$, this is $\tau = \pi m = \pi G_NM/c^3$, about $1.5 \times 10^{-4}\,$s for ten solar masses; any other motion inside
reaches $r = 0$ sooner, so firing a rocket only shortens the remaining time [@blennow2022relativity, Problems 2.91 and 2.96].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Eddington-Finkelstein form follows from the Schwarzschild form by a change of coordinate. The first exercise
carries it out and identifies the ingoing light rays.

::: {#exr-gr-horizon-ef}
#### Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates

Show that $dr_*/dr = (1 - 2m/r)^{-1}$, substitute $dt = dv - dr/(1 - 2m/r)$ in @eq-gr-schwarzschild, and obtain
@eq-gr-eddington-finkelstein. Which curves are the ingoing light rays?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tfrac{d}{dr}\bigl(r + 2m\log|r/2m - 1|\bigr) = 1 + \tfrac{2m}{r - 2m} = \tfrac{r}{r - 2m}$. With $f = 1 - 2m/r$, $f(dv - dr/f)^2 - dr^2/f =
f\,dv^2 - 2dv\,dr$: the $dr^2$ terms cancel, and the metric coefficients are smooth at $f = 0$. Ingoing radial light
rays are the lines $v = \text{constant}$, since then $ds^2 = 0$ with $d\Omega = 0$.
:::

A falling observer reaches the horizon and the centre in finite proper time. The second exercise computes it for a
fall from rest at infinity.

::: {#exr-gr-horizon-infall-time}
#### Falling in

For radial free fall from rest at infinity, $E = 1$ and $L = 0$, show that $(dr/d\tau)^2 = 2m/r$ and compute the proper
time from $r = 2m$ to $r = 0$. Show that the coordinate time $t$ diverges near $r = 2m$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The normalisation $g(u, u) = 1$ with $E = (1 - 2m/r)\dot t$ gives $\dot r^2 = E^2 - (1 - 2m/r) = 2m/r$, exactly the
Newtonian energy equation. Then $\tau = \int_0^{2m}\sqrt{r/2m}\,dr = 4m/3$: about $66\,\mu$s for a black hole of ten solar
masses. Near $r = 2m(1 + \varepsilon)$, $|dt/dr| \approx 1/\varepsilon + \tfrac32$, and with $dr = 2m\,d\varepsilon$ the coordinate time grows like
$t \approx -2m\log\varepsilon \to \infty$.

```python
m, r, r0 = var('m r r0'); assume(m > 0, r > 0, r0 > 2*m)
f = 1 - 2*m/r
print("E = 1, L = 0 give (dr/dtau)^2 = E^2 - f =", (1 - f).simplify_full())
tau = integrate(sqrt(r/(2*m)), r, 0, 2*m)
print("proper time from the horizon to r = 0:", tau)
dtdr = 1/(f*sqrt(2*m/r))
eps = var('eps'); assume(eps > 0)
print("near r = 2m(1 + eps), |dt/dr| ~", dtdr.subs(r=2*m*(1 + eps)).series(eps, 1).truncate().canonicalize_radical(), " so t ~ -2m log(eps): diverges")
```

*Output:*

```text
E = 1, L = 0 give (dr/dtau)^2 = E^2 - f = 2*m/r
proper time from the horizon to r = 0: 4/3*m
near r = 2m(1 + eps), |dt/dr| ~ 1/2*(3*eps + 2)/eps  so t ~ -2m log(eps): diverges
```
:::

Black holes are not completely black once quantum mechanics is included. The third exercise quotes the result and
relates it to the redshift at the horizon.

::: {#exr-gr-horizon-temperature}
#### Surface gravity and temperature

The **surface gravity** $\kappa_s$ is the redshifted acceleration needed to hold a static observer at the horizon,
$\kappa_s = \tfrac12f'(r_s)$ for $f = 1 - 2m/r$. Compute it, and evaluate Hawking's temperature $T_H = \kappa_s/2\pi$ (in units
$\hbar = c = k_B = G_N = 1$, quoted, not derived here) for a black hole of one solar mass, using $T_H = 6.2 \times
10^{-8}\,\mathrm{K}\,(M_\odot/M)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f'(r) = 2m/r^2$, so $\kappa_s = m/r_s^2 = 1/(4m)$ and $T_H = 1/(8\pi m)$: larger black holes are colder. For one solar mass
$T_H = 6.2 \times 10^{-8}\,$K, far below the $2.7\,$K of the cosmic microwave background, so astrophysical black holes
absorb more than they radiate.
:::

The Kruskal coordinates cover the interior as well as the exterior. The next exercise uses them to show that nothing
leaves the black-hole region, which is the content of the word horizon.

::: {#exr-grb-kruskal-trapped}
#### No way out

In the Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates $ds^2 = \tfrac{16m^2}{r}e^{(2m - r)/2m}\,du\,dv - r^2d\Omega^2$ with $uv = (2m - r)e^{(r - 2m)/2m}$ and
$t = 2m\log(-v/u)$ outside, show that future-directed causal curves have $\dot u \geq 0$, $\dot v \geq 0$, that $uv$ is a decreasing function of $r$,
and conclude that a curve entering the region $u > 0$, $v > 0$ never returns to $r > 2m$ [@blennow2022relativity, Problems 2.107-2.108].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A causal curve has $\tfrac{16m^2}{r}e^{(2m - r)/2m}\dot u\dot v \geq r^2\dot\Omega^2 \geq 0$, so $\dot u$ and $\dot v$ have the same sign (or one vanishes); in the
exterior $u < 0 < v$, increasing $t$ at fixed $r$ means $-v/u$ increasing at fixed $uv$, that is $u$ and $v$ increasing, which fixes
the future direction everywhere by continuity. $\tfrac{d}{dr}\bigl[(2m - r)e^{(r - 2m)/2m}\bigr] = -\tfrac{r}{2m}e^{(r - 2m)/2m} < 0$. In the region $u, v > 0$,
$\tfrac{d}{d\sigma}(uv) = \dot uv + u\dot v \geq 0$, so $uv$ does not decrease and $r$ does not increase along the curve; since $r > 2m$ would need
$uv < 0$, the curve stays at $r < 2m$, and reaches $r = 0$ at $uv = 2m/e$.
:::
::::

The geometry of the solution and the motion in it fit in one proposition. It collects the exact statements on
curvature, light cones and geodesics, and the two classic effects, the perihelion advance and light deflection.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-gr-schwarzschild}
#### Geodesics of the Schwarzschild metric

With $G_N = 1$ and $m = M$: (a) @eq-gr-schwarzschild is Ricci flat and its Kretschmann scalar is
$R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = 48m^2/r^6$; (b) radial light rays have $dr/dt = \pm(1 - 2m/r)$, the metric in $(v, r)$ is
@eq-gr-eddington-finkelstein, and the outgoing slope $(1 + 2m/r)/(1 - 2m/r)$ in the $(r, v - r)$ plane is negative inside
$r = 2m$; (c) for a geodesic in the plane $\theta = \pi/2$ with conserved $E = (1 - 2m/r)\dot t$ and $L = r^2\dot\varphi$, the radial
equation is $\ddot r = -\tfrac12V'(r)$ with
$$
V(r) = \Bigl(1 - \frac{2m}{r}\Bigr)\Bigl(1 + \frac{L^2}{r^2}\Bigr), \qquad \dot r^2 = E^2 - V(r),
$$ {#eq-gr-schwarzschild-potential}
circular orbits satisfy $mr^2 - L^2r + 3mL^2 = 0$, the innermost stable one is at $r = 6m$ with $L^2 = 12m^2$, and $u = 1/r$
obeys the orbit equation $u'' + u = m/L^2 + 3mu^2$; (d) numerically, the perihelion advances per revolution by
$6\pi m/p$, $p = L^2/m$, to within $3\%$ for $p = 300m$, $1000m$, $3000m$, and light passing at impact parameter $b$ is deflected
by $4m/b$ to within $5\%$ for $b = 200m$, $1000m$, $5000m$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![The Schwarzschild solution ($G_N = 1$). Left: radial light cones in the ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein plane $(r, v -
r)$; outside the horizon (blue) the outgoing edge points to larger $r$, at $r = 2m$ it is vertical, and inside (red) both
edges point to smaller $r$; centre: a bound geodesic with turning points $p/(1 \pm e)$, $p = 40m$, $e = 0.5$, over four
revolutions (red), precessing about the ellipse with the same turning points (blue, dashed); right: light rays with
impact parameters $6m$ to $20m$, bent by the mass; the ray at $b = 6m$, just above the critical $3\sqrt3\,m$, swings
around the hole.](figures/schwarzschild.svg){#fig-schwarzschild width=100%}

{{< interactive schwarzschild 460 >}}

The interactive version varies the parameter $p$ of the bound geodesic. The perihelion advance of Mercury was the first success of the theory. The example evaluates the formula of the
proposition with the orbit of Mercury.

::: {#exm-gr-mercury}
#### The perihelion of Mercury

Restoring units, the advance per orbit is $6\pi G_NM_\odot/(c^2a(1 - e^2))$ with $a = 5.79 \times 10^{10}\,$m and $e = 0.206$:
$5.0 \times 10^{-7}\,$rad. Mercury completes $415$ orbits per century, giving $2.1 \times 10^{-4}\,$rad $= 43''$ per
century, the anomaly that Newtonian perturbations by the other planets could not explain.
:::

The deflection of light by the Sun was measured during the eclipse of 1919. The formula of the proposition gives the
value for a ray grazing the solar surface.

::: {#exm-gr-light-bending}
#### Light bending by the Sun

For $b = R_\odot = 6.96 \times 10^8\,$m, $4G_NM_\odot/(c^2R_\odot) = 4 \times 1476\,\mathrm{m}/6.96 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{m} = 8.5 \times
10^{-6}\,$rad $= 1.75''$, twice the Newtonian value (@exr-gr-nl-light), as confirmed by the eclipse expedition and by
radio interferometry to better than $10^{-3}$.
:::

Close to the hole the orbits behave differently from Kepler's. Two radii mark the change, the innermost stable orbit
and the photon sphere.

::: {#exm-gr-isco}
#### The innermost stable orbit

Circular orbits exist down to $r = 3m$ and are stable only for $r \geq 6m$, where the two roots of $mr^2 - L^2r + 3mL^2 =
0$ merge. Matter in an accretion disc spirals in through stable orbits and plunges from $r = 6m$, having radiated the
fraction $1 - \sqrt{8/9} = 5.7\%$ of its rest energy (@exr-gr-isco-energy), far more than nuclear fusion releases.
:::

Kepler's third law survives in the Schwarzschild metric in a surprisingly exact form. The next example derives it and
the proper time of the orbiting body, which is not given by the same law.

::: {#exm-grb-kepler-exact}
#### Kepler's third law in Schwarzschild coordinates

For a circular geodesic $r = r_0$, $\ddot r = 0$ and the $r$-component of the geodesic equation reduces to $\Gamma^r_{tt}\dot t^2 + \Gamma^r_{\varphi\varphi}\dot\varphi^2 = 0$,
that is $(m/r_0^2)(1 - 2m/r_0)\dot t^2 = r_0(1 - 2m/r_0)\dot\varphi^2$. Hence $(d\varphi/dt)^2 = m/r_0^3$ exactly, and the coordinate period is
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{r_0^3/G_NM}$, Kepler's law with no correction. The proper period is shorter: $d\tau^2 = (1 - 2m/r_0 - r_0^2\Omega^2)dt^2$ gives
$\tau = T\sqrt{1 - 3m/r_0}$, real only above the photon sphere $r_0 = 3m$ [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.72].
:::

The photon sphere also sets the size of the black hole as seen from far away. The next example converts the critical
impact parameter of @exr-gr-photon-sphere into a cross-section.

::: {#exm-grb-capture}
#### The optical size of a black hole

Light from infinity with impact parameter $b < b_c = 3\sqrt3\,m$ is captured, and light with $b > b_c$ escapes. A black hole
therefore absorbs a beam over the area $\sigma = \pi b_c^2 = 27\pi G_N^2M^2/c^4$, and looks like a dark disc of radius $b_c \approx 2.6r_s$, larger
than its horizon by the lensing of rays that pass close to it. For the black hole M87* with $M = 6.5 \times 10^9M_\odot$ at $16.8\,$Mpc this
radius subtends about $20\,\mu$as, the scale of the shadow imaged in 2019 [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.76].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Light has its own effective potential, obtained from @eq-gr-schwarzschild-potential by dropping the rest mass. The
first exercise finds its maximum.

::: {#exr-gr-photon-sphere}
#### The photon sphere

For null geodesics $\dot r^2 = E^2 - (1 - 2m/r)L^2/r^2$. Find the radius of the unstable circular light orbit and the
critical impact parameter $b_c = L/E$ below which light is captured.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$W(r) = (1 - 2m/r)/r^2$ has $W' = 0$ at $r = 3m$, a maximum with $W(3m) = 1/(27m^2)$. A ray with $1/b^2 = E^2/L^2 >
1/(27m^2)$ passes over the barrier and falls in, so $b_c = 3\sqrt3\,m \approx 5.2m$; this is the size of the shadow of a black
hole as imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope.

```python
m, r = var('m r'); assume(m > 0, r > 0)
W = (1 - 2*m/r)/r^2
crit = solve(diff(W, r) == 0, r)
print("critical points of (1 - 2m/r)/r^2:", crit, "; second derivative there:", diff(W, r, 2).subs(crit[0]).simplify_full())
print("maximum value:", W.subs(crit[0]), "; critical impact parameter b_c = 1/sqrt(max):", sqrt(1/W.subs(crit[0])).simplify_full(), "=", (3*sqrt(3)).n(digits=5), "m")
```

*Output:*

```text
critical points of (1 - 2m/r)/r^2: [
r == 3*m
] ; second derivative there: -2/81/m^4
maximum value: 1/27/m^2 ; critical impact parameter b_c = 1/sqrt(max): 3*sqrt(3)*m = 5.1962 m
```
:::

The energy and angular momentum of circular orbits follow from @eq-gr-schwarzschild-potential. The second exercise
computes them and the binding energy at the innermost stable orbit.

::: {#exr-gr-isco-energy}
#### Energy of circular orbits

Show that a circular geodesic of radius $r > 3m$ has $L^2 = mr^2/(r - 3m)$ and $E^2 = (1 - 2m/r)^2/(1 - 3m/r)$, evaluate $E$
at $r = 6m$, and expand $E - 1$ at large $r$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$V'(r) = 0$ is linear in $L^2$ and gives $L^2 = mr^2/(r - 3m)$; then $E^2 = V(r)$ simplifies to $(1 - 2m/r)^2/(1 - 3m/r)$. At
$r = 6m$, $E = \sqrt{8/9} = 0.943$; at large $r$, $E - 1 \approx -m/(2r)$, the Newtonian energy of a circular orbit per unit
mass.

```python
m, r, L2 = var('m r L2'); assume(m > 0, r > 3*m)
V = (1 - 2*m/r)*(1 + L2/r^2)
L2c = solve(diff(V, r) == 0, L2)[0].rhs()
E2 = V.subs(L2=L2c).simplify_full()
print("L^2 =", L2c.factor(), "; E^2 =", E2.factor(), "; equals (1 - 2m/r)^2/(1 - 3m/r):", bool((E2 - (1 - 2*m/r)^2/(1 - 3*m/r)).simplify_full() == 0))
Eisco = sqrt(E2.subs(r=6*m))
print("at r = 6m: E =", Eisco, "; binding energy fraction 1 - E =", (1 - Eisco).n(digits=4))
print("large r: E - 1 ~", (sqrt(E2) - 1).subs(r=1/var('u')).taylor(var('u'), 0, 1), " (the Newtonian -m/(2r))")
```

*Output:*

```text
L^2 = -m*r^2/(3*m - r) ; E^2 = -(2*m - r)^2/((3*m - r)*r) ; equals (1 - 2m/r)^2/(1 - 3m/r): True
at r = 6m: E = 2/3*sqrt(2) ; binding energy fraction 1 - E = 0.05719
large r: E - 1 ~ -1/2*m*u  (the Newtonian -m/(2r))
```
:::

The precession can also be found by perturbation theory instead of numerics. The third exercise derives the
coefficient $6\pi m/p$.

::: {#exr-gr-perihelion-perturbative}
#### The perihelion advance by perturbation theory

Write the orbit equation as $u'' + u = 1/p + 3mu^2$ with $p = L^2/m$ and treat $3mu^2$ as small. Show that $u = \tfrac1p(1 +
e\cos((1 - \varepsilon)\varphi))$ solves it to first order in $m/p$ and in $e$, with $\varepsilon = 3m/p$, and deduce the advance $6\pi m/p$
per revolution.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Substituting, $u'' + u = \tfrac1p + \tfrac ep(1 - (1 - \varepsilon)^2)\cos((1 - \varepsilon)\varphi) \approx \tfrac1p + \tfrac{2\varepsilon e}{p}\cos(\dots)$, while
$3mu^2 \approx \tfrac{3m}{p^2}(1 + 2e\cos(\dots))$. The cosine terms match for $2\varepsilon = 6m/p$, and the constant $3m/p^2$ only
shifts $p$ slightly. Perihelia ($u$ maximal) occur at $(1 - \varepsilon)\varphi = 2\pi k$, i.e. every $2\pi/(1 - \varepsilon) \approx 2\pi(1 +
\varepsilon)$: the advance per revolution is $2\pi\varepsilon = 6\pi m/p$, the value checked numerically in @prp-gr-schwarzschild.
:::

Clocks on circular orbits run differently from clocks at rest at the same radius. The next exercise compares them for
an orbit like that of the GPS satellites, with Sage.

::: {#exr-grb-orbit-vs-static}
#### An orbiting clock and a static clock

At radius $r_0$ in the Schwarzschild metric ($G_N = c = 1$, $r_s = 2m$) a satellite moves on a circular geodesic and a static observer hovers.
With Sage: (a) write the satellite's four-velocity as $U = \alpha\partial_t + \beta\partial_\varphi$ and find $\alpha$, $\beta$; (b) find their relative speed from
$\gamma = g(U, V)$; (c) find the ratio of the times that their clocks show between two meetings; (d) evaluate for $r_s = 8.87\,$mm and
$r_0 = 26\,560\,$km [@blennow2022relativity, Problems 2.99 and 2.100].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\Omega = d\varphi/dt = \sqrt{m/r_0^3}$ from @exm-grb-kepler-exact, $\alpha = (1 - 3r_s/2r_0)^{-1/2}$ and $\beta = \alpha\Omega$:

```python
r0, rs = var('r0 rs'); assume(r0 > 3 * rs / 2, rs > 0)
f = 1 - rs / r0
Om = sqrt(rs / (2 * r0^3))                       # dphi/dt on a circular geodesic (Kepler's law, exact)
alpha = 1 / sqrt(f - r0^2 * Om^2)                # dt/dtau from g(U, U) = 1
beta = alpha * Om
print("alpha^2 = 1/(1 - 3 rs/(2 r0)):", bool((alpha^2 - 1 / (1 - 3 * rs / (2 * r0))).simplify_full() == 0))
print("normalisation f alpha^2 - r0^2 beta^2 = 1:", bool((f * alpha^2 - r0^2 * beta^2).simplify_full() == 1))
gam = (f * alpha * (1 / sqrt(f))).simplify_full()   # g(U, V) with V = f^(-1/2) d_t
v = sqrt(1 - 1 / gam^2).simplify_full()
print("relative speed v^2 =", (v^2).factor(), "  equals rs/(2 (r0 - rs)):", bool((v^2 - rs / (2 * (r0 - rs))).simplify_full() == 0))
ratio = (sqrt(1 - 3 * rs / (2 * r0)) / sqrt(f))
print("tau_orbit/tau_static = 1/gamma:", bool((ratio - 1 / gam).simplify_full() == 0))
num = {rs: 8.87e-3, r0: 2.656e7}
print("GPS: v = %.1f m/s, 1 - tau_orbit/tau_static = %.3e" % (v.subs(num) * 3e8, 1 - ratio.subs(num)))
print("GPS: one orbit takes %.2f h of coordinate time" % ((2 * pi / Om).subs(num) / 3e8 / 3600))
```

*Output:*

```text
alpha^2 = 1/(1 - 3 rs/(2 r0)): True
normalisation f alpha^2 - r0^2 beta^2 = 1: True
relative speed v^2 = 1/2*rs/(r0 - rs)   equals rs/(2 (r0 - rs)): True
tau_orbit/tau_static = 1/gamma: True
GPS: v = 3876.6 m/s, 1 - tau_orbit/tau_static = 8.349e-11
GPS: one orbit takes 11.96 h of coordinate time
```

The relative speed is $v = \sqrt{r_s/2(r_0 - r_s)}$, the Newtonian orbital speed corrected by the static observer's clock, and the
orbiting clock falls behind by the factor $1/\gamma$: $8 \times 10^{-11}$, about $7\,\mu$s per day, the special-relativistic part of the GPS
correction of @exr-gr-gps-clock.
:::

A slightly perturbed circular orbit oscillates radially, and the oscillation is slower than the orbit. The next
exercise computes the ratio of the two periods, which is the perihelion advance in another form.

::: {#exr-grb-epicycles}
#### Radial oscillations about a circular orbit

For a geodesic close to the circular orbit $r = r_0$, write $r = r_0 + \rho$ and use @eq-gr-schwarzschild-potential to show with Sage that $\rho$ oscillates
with $\omega_r^2 = \tfrac12V''(r_0)$, and that the ratio of the radial period to the orbital period is $(1 - 6m/r_0)^{-1/2}$. Deduce the perihelion
advance per orbit for $r_0 \gg m$ [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.75].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating $\dot r^2 = E^2 - V$ gives $\ddot\rho = -\tfrac12V''(r_0)\rho$; both frequencies are taken in proper time, so their ratio is
independent of the time used:

```python
r, r0, m, L = var('r r0 m L'); assume(r0 > 6 * m, m > 0)
V = (1 - 2 * m / r) * (1 + L^2 / r^2)
L2 = solve(diff(V, r).subs(r=r0) == 0, L^2)[0].rhs()
print("circular orbit: L^2 =", L2.factor())
wr2 = (diff(V, r, 2).subs(r=r0) / 2).subs(L^2 == L2).simplify_full()
wphi2 = (L2 / r0^4).simplify_full()               # (dphi/dtau)^2 on the circular orbit
ratio2 = (wphi2 / wr2).simplify_full()
print("(T_r/T_phi)^2 =", ratio2.factor(), "  equals 1/(1 - 6m/r0):", bool((ratio2 - 1 / (1 - 6 * m / r0)).simplify_full() == 0))
eps = var('eps')
adv = taylor(2 * pi * (sqrt(ratio2.subs(m=eps * r0)) - 1), eps, 0, 1)
print("perihelion advance per orbit to first order in m/r0:", adv.subs(eps=m / r0))
print("Mercury: 6 pi GM/(c^2 a) per orbit = %.3e rad (a = 5.79e10 m)" % (6 * pi.n() * 1476.6 / 5.79e10))
```

*Output:*

```text
circular orbit: L^2 = -m*r0^2/(3*m - r0)
(T_r/T_phi)^2 = -r0/(6*m - r0)   equals 1/(1 - 6m/r0): True
perihelion advance per orbit to first order in m/r0: 6*pi*m/r0
Mercury: 6 pi GM/(c^2 a) per orbit = 4.807e-07 rad (a = 5.79e10 m)
```

The radial period exceeds the orbital one, so the perihelion comes back after the angle $2\pi(1 - 6m/r_0)^{-1/2} \approx 2\pi + 6\pi m/r_0$,
the advance of @exm-gr-mercury for a circular orbit. At $r_0 = 6m$ the radial frequency vanishes: the innermost stable orbit.
:::
::::

### Symmetries and conserved quantities

The orbits of @prp-gr-schwarzschild were found from two constants of motion, $E$ and $L$, which @exr-gr-int-particle-orbits traced back to the independence of the metric on $t$ and $\varphi$. The mechanism is general. A Killing vector field (@def-killing, @sec-killing) is the generator of a continuous family of isometries, and each one gives a quantity conserved by free particles and by light, a quantity conserved by charged particles in a field that shares the symmetry, and a conserved current for any matter with a conserved stress tensor. This unit collects the three statements in one proposition, which is the tool behind the classical tests of the next unit, the charged black holes after it, and the charge of Kaluza-Klein theory. The sources are @emam2021covariant [Sec. 6.1.3], @plebanski2024introduction [Sec. 21.7] and @blennow2022relativity [Problems 2.63-2.69].

The proof needs only Killing's equation $\nabla_\mu K_\nu + \nabla_\nu K_\mu = 0$ and the geodesic equation of @def-geodesic. The proposition fixes the sign conventions used below: in our signature the energy is $+g(\partial_t, u)$ and the angular momentum is $-g(\partial_\varphi, u)$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-grf-killing-conserved}
#### Conserved quantities of a Killing vector

Let $K$ be a Killing vector field of the spacetime metric $g$ (@def-killing).

1. Along every affinely parametrised geodesic $x(\lambda)$, timelike or null, $Q_K = g(K, \dot x) = K_\mu\dot x^\mu$ is constant.
2. A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ obeying $m\,u^\nu\nabla_\nu u^\mu = qF^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu$, the Lorentz force of @prp-sr-lorentz-force on a curved spacetime, in a field $F = dA$ whose potential is preserved by the flow of $K$, $\mathcal{L}_KA = 0$, conserves $m\,g(K, u) + q\,A(K) = mK_\mu u^\mu + qK^\mu A_\mu$.
3. If $T^{\mu\nu}$ is symmetric and conserved, $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = 0$, the current $J^\mu = T^{\mu\nu}K_\nu$ is conserved, $\nabla_\mu J^\mu = \frac{1}{\sqrt{-g}}\partial_\mu(\sqrt{-g}\,J^\mu) = 0$; when $J$ vanishes at spatial infinity, $Q = \int\sqrt{-g}\,J^0\,d^3x$ over a slice $x^0 = \text{const}$ does not depend on $x^0$.

*Proof.* (1) $\frac{d}{d\lambda}(K_\mu\dot x^\mu) = \dot x^\nu\nabla_\nu(K_\mu\dot x^\mu) = \dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu\nabla_\nu K_\mu + K_\mu\dot x^\nu\nabla_\nu\dot x^\mu$. The first term contracts a symmetric product with $\nabla_\nu K_\mu$, which is antisymmetric by Killing's equation, and the second vanishes by the geodesic equation. (2) As in (1), $\frac{d}{d\tau}(mK_\mu u^\mu) = qK_\mu F^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu = qK^\mu F_{\mu\nu}u^\nu$. The Lie derivative $(\mathcal{L}_KA)_\nu = K^\mu\partial_\mu A_\nu + A_\mu\partial_\nu K^\mu$ vanishes, so $\frac{d}{d\tau}(K^\mu A_\mu) = u^\nu(\partial_\nu K^\mu)A_\mu + u^\nu K^\mu\partial_\nu A_\mu = u^\nu K^\mu(\partial_\nu A_\mu - \partial_\mu A_\nu) = K^\mu F_{\nu\mu}u^\nu$, and the two derivatives cancel. (3) $\nabla_\mu(T^{\mu\nu}K_\nu) = K_\nu\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu} + T^{\mu\nu}\nabla_\mu K_\nu = 0$, the second term again pairing a symmetric with an antisymmetric tensor. Integrating $\partial_\mu(\sqrt{-g}J^\mu) = 0$ over the region between two slices and dropping the boundary at infinity gives the constancy of $Q$ [@emam2021covariant, eqs. 6.35-6.40; @plebanski2024introduction, Sec. 21.7; @blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.63]. $\square$
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is flat spacetime, where the Killing vectors are the generators of the Poincaré group and the conserved quantities are the familiar ones. The boost is the instructive case, because its conserved quantity depends explicitly on time.

::: {#exm-grf-kc-minkowski}
#### The Poincaré charges of a free particle

In Minkowski spacetime the translations $\partial_t$, $\partial_i$ give $g(\partial_t, p) = p^0$ and $g(\partial_i, p) = -p^i$ for a particle of four-momentum $p = m\dot x$: energy and momentum are conserved. The rotation $x\partial_y - y\partial_x$ gives $-(xp^y - yp^x)$, the angular momentum. The boost $K = x\partial_t + t\partial_x$ gives $g(K, p) = xp^0 - tp^x$; its constancy says $x = (p^x/p^0)\,t + \text{const}$, uniform motion of the particle [@emam2021covariant, Sec. 6.1.3].
:::

The Schwarzschild metric has fewer symmetries than flat spacetime, and the conserved quantities used in @prp-gr-schwarzschild are those of its four Killing vectors. Two of them were used explicitly there; the other two fixed the plane of the orbit.

::: {#exm-grf-kc-schwarzschild}
#### Energy and angular momentum in the Schwarzschild metric

The components of @eq-gr-schwarzschild do not depend on $t$ and $\varphi$, so $\partial_t$ and $\partial_\varphi$ are Killing, with $E = g(\partial_t, u) = (1 - 2m/r)\dot t$ and $L = -g(\partial_\varphi, u) = r^2\sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi$. The two other rotation generators of @prp-sphere-killing are Killing as well; their conserved quantities are the other components of the angular momentum, so its direction is fixed and the orbit stays in a plane, which a rotation takes to $\theta = \pi/2$ [@emam2021covariant, Exercise 6.10].
:::

Part (1) of the proposition holds for null geodesics too, where the affine parameter has no physical normalisation. The ratios of conserved quantities are then the meaningful numbers.

::: {#exm-grf-kc-impact-parameter}
#### The impact parameter of a light ray

For a light ray the affine parameter can be rescaled, $\lambda \to c\lambda$, which multiplies $E$ and $L$ by $1/c$. Their ratio $b = L/E$ does not change: it is the impact parameter, the distance at which the ray would pass the centre if it were not bent, since for $r \to \infty$, $L/E = r^2\dot\varphi/\dot t \to r^2\,d\varphi/dt$, which is $b$ for a straight line. This is the $b$ of the light bending and capture results of @prp-gr-schwarzschild and @exm-grb-capture.
:::

A spacetime with less symmetry still has conserved quantities if some symmetry is left. The expanding universe has no time translation, but it keeps the spatial ones, and they explain why motion relative to the expansion dies out.

::: {#exm-grf-kc-flrw}
#### Momentum in an expanding universe

The flat FLRW metric $dt^2 - a(t)^2d\mathbf x^2$ (@def-gr-flrw-metric) has the Killing vectors $\partial_i$ but $\partial_t$ is not Killing. For a particle of mass $m$, $g(\partial_x, p) = -ma^2\dot x$ is conserved. The momentum measured by a comoving observer is $|\mathbf p|_{\text{phys}} = ma|\dot{\mathbf x}|$, so $|\mathbf p|_{\text{phys}} \propto 1/a$: peculiar momenta decay as the universe expands, as found for de Sitter space in @exr-gr-ds-peculiar. Energy is not conserved, because there is no timelike Killing vector.
:::

Part (2) applies to a charge in a magnetic field, where the conserved quantity is not the mechanical angular momentum. The gauge has to be chosen so that the potential, not only the field, is symmetric.

::: {#exm-grf-kc-magnetic}
#### Canonical angular momentum in a magnetic field

A uniform magnetic field $B$ along $z$ in Minkowski spacetime has the symmetric-gauge potential $\mathbf A = \frac B2(-y, x, 0)$, that is $A_x = \frac B2y$, $A_y = -\frac B2x$ in our signature, and $\mathcal{L}_KA = 0$ for the rotation $K = x\partial_y - y\partial_x$. Part (2) gives the constant $-m(xu^y - yu^x) - \frac{qB}{2}(x^2 + y^2)$: up to sign, the mechanical angular momentum plus $\frac{qB}{2}\rho^2$, the canonical angular momentum of a charge in a magnetic field. In the Landau gauge $\mathbf A = (0, Bx, 0)$ the field is the same but the potential is not rotation invariant, and the mechanical angular momentum alone is not conserved.
:::

Part (3) turns a symmetry of spacetime into a conserved total charge of a field. In flat spacetime it recovers the energy and momentum of the electromagnetic field.

::: {#exm-grf-kc-field-energy}
#### The energy and momentum of the electromagnetic field

In Minkowski spacetime with the Maxwell stress tensor of @exm-stress-maxwell, $K = \partial_t$ gives $J^\mu = T^{\mu0}$ and $Q = \int T^{00}d^3x = \int\frac12(\mathbf E^2 + \mathbf B^2)\,d^3x$, and $K = \partial_i$ gives $J^0 = -T^{0i}$, so $Q = -\int(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)_i\,d^3x$ (@exr-gr-maxwell-stress). The conservation $\partial_\mu J^\mu = 0$ for $K = \partial_t$ is Poynting's theorem in empty space (@prp-emm-poynting).
:::

A vector field that is not Killing gives no conservation law. The radial direction of the Schwarzschild metric is the standard example, and it matches Newtonian intuition.

::: {#exm-grf-kc-radial}
#### No radial conservation law

In the Schwarzschild metric $g_{tt}$ and $g_{rr}$ depend on $r$, so $\mathcal{L}_{\partial_r}g \neq 0$ and $\partial_r$ is not Killing. Accordingly $g(\partial_r, u) = -\dot r/(1 - 2m/r)$ changes along a radial fall, as it must: a falling body is accelerated, and in Newtonian terms its radial momentum is not conserved because the force is radial [@emam2021covariant, Sec. 6.1.3].
:::

In Kaluza-Klein theory a fifth dimension is a circle, and its translation is a Killing vector. Part (1) then gives a conserved quantity which, seen from four dimensions, is an electric charge.

::: {#exm-grf-kc-kaluza-klein}
#### The charge of Kaluza-Klein theory

On $M_4 \times S^1$ with $ds^2 = g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - (dy + A_\mu dx^\mu)^2$, the components do not depend on $y$, so $\partial_y$ is Killing and $p_y = g(\partial_y, \dot x) = -(\dot y + A_\mu\dot x^\mu)$ is constant along five-dimensional geodesics. Part III of the Kaluza-Klein tutorial shows that the four-dimensional projection of such a geodesic obeys the Lorentz force law with a charge proportional to $p_y$: momentum around the circle is charge, and part (2) of the proposition is the four-dimensional shadow of part (1).
:::

The static patch of de Sitter space has a timelike Killing vector, but only inside its horizon. Its conserved energy shows the repulsive effect of a positive cosmological constant on radial motion.

::: {#exm-grf-kc-de-sitter}
#### Radial motion in the static patch of de Sitter space

The static metric $(1 - H^2r^2)dt^2 - (1 - H^2r^2)^{-1}dr^2 - r^2d\Omega^2$ of @exr-gr-int-de-sitter-three-ways has the Killing vector $\partial_t$, timelike for $r < 1/H$. A radial timelike geodesic conserves $E = (1 - H^2r^2)\dot t$, and $g(u, u) = 1$ gives $\dot r^2 = E^2 - 1 + H^2r^2$. Differentiating, $\ddot r = H^2r$: free particles separate exponentially in proper time, the local form of the expansion of @exm-gr-ds-hubble.
:::

How many conserved quantities a spacetime has decides how far its geodesics can be integrated by quadratures. The count combines the Killing vectors with the conserved length of the tangent vector.

::: {#exm-grf-kc-counting}
#### Counting first integrals

Along any geodesic $g(\dot x, \dot x)$ is constant, whether or not there are Killing vectors. Minkowski and de Sitter space have ten Killing vectors, more than enough to integrate geodesics completely. The Schwarzschild metric has four, $\partial_t$ and three rotations; with $g(\dot x, \dot x)$ they reduce the motion to the single radial equation of @eq-gr-schwarzschild-potential. The rotating Kerr black hole has only two Killing vectors, $\partial_t$ and $\partial_\varphi$, and its geodesics are integrable only thanks to a fourth constant found by Carter that does not come from a Killing vector [@plebanski2024introduction, Sec. 21.7].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises begin with the proof of part (1) written out in coordinates, as Blennow and Ohlsson pose it. It uses the symmetry of the Christoffel symbols instead of the covariant derivative.

::: {#exr-grf-kc-coordinates}
#### The conservation law in coordinates

Using the geodesic equation $\ddot x^\rho = -\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu$ and Killing's equation in the form @eq-killing, show directly that $\frac{d}{d\lambda}(g_{\mu\nu}K^\mu\dot x^\nu) = 0$ [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.63].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{d}{d\lambda}(g_{\mu\nu}K^\mu\dot x^\nu) = \partial_\rho g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\rho K^\mu\dot x^\nu + g_{\mu\nu}\partial_\rho K^\mu\dot x^\rho\dot x^\nu - g_{\mu\nu}K^\mu\Gamma^\nu_{\alpha\beta}\dot x^\alpha\dot x^\beta$. With $g_{\mu\nu}\Gamma^\nu_{\alpha\beta} = \frac12(\partial_\alpha g_{\mu\beta} + \partial_\beta g_{\mu\alpha} - \partial_\mu g_{\alpha\beta})$ and the symmetry in $\alpha, \beta$, the last term is $-K^\mu\dot x^\alpha\dot x^\beta(\partial_\alpha g_{\mu\beta} - \frac12\partial_\mu g_{\alpha\beta})$. The first and this term combine to $\frac12K^\mu\partial_\mu g_{\alpha\beta}\dot x^\alpha\dot x^\beta$, and the middle term is $\frac12(g_{\mu\beta}\partial_\alpha K^\mu + g_{\alpha\mu}\partial_\beta K^\mu)\dot x^\alpha\dot x^\beta$. The sum is $\frac12\dot x^\alpha\dot x^\beta$ times the left side of @eq-killing, which vanishes.
:::

The second exercise applies part (1) to a curved surface, where the conservation law is Clairaut's relation. It confirms the law by integrating a geodesic numerically.

::: {#exr-grf-kc-paraboloid}
#### Geodesics on a paraboloid

The paraboloid $z = \alpha(x^2 + y^2)$ has the induced metric $(1 + 4\alpha^2r^2)dr^2 + r^2d\varphi^2$. (a) Show that $\partial_\varphi$ is Killing and find the conserved quantity. (b) For a geodesic of unit speed, find the smallest radius it reaches. (c) With Sage, integrate a geodesic and check the conservation [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.66].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) The components do not depend on $\varphi$, so $\partial_\varphi$ is Killing and $\ell = r^2\dot\varphi$ is conserved. (b) Unit speed gives $(1 + 4\alpha^2r^2)\dot r^2 + \ell^2/r^2 = 1$, so $\dot r = 0$ requires $r = |\ell|$: the geodesic comes in to $r_{\min} = |\ell|$ and goes out again, never reaching the vertex unless $\ell = 0$. (c) For $\alpha = 1$ and a geodesic starting at $r = 2$ at the angle $60°$ to the radial direction:

```python
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
import numpy as np
r, ph = var('r ph'); al = 1
g = matrix([[1 + 4*al^2*r^2, 0], [0, r^2]])
gi = g.inverse(); X = [r, ph]
```
